newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya's Moi, religious leaders discuss reforms.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's Moi, religious leaders discuss reforms.

text.p: President Daniel arap Moi met Kenya's religious leaders on Tuesday and agreed on the need for constitutional reforms, a conciliatory gesture in the face of an opposition-backed campaign which has led to bloody clashes between police and demonstrators.

The official Presidential Press Service (PPS) said Moi and religious leaders agreed it was necessary to review the constitution "with a view to amending or overhauling it to serve the needs, requirements and aspirations of modern Kenya".
But it added: "The time and mechanism for effecting these changes will be discussed in subsequent meetings."
The meeting at State House, Nairobi, was the president's first with religious leaders on reforms since the start of an opposition-backed campaign pressing for change.
The PPS said Moi and the clerics, including Kenya's Catholic and Anglican archbishops and its chief Moslem Kadhi, agreed violence should be condemned and confrontation eliminated.
It said Moi's government would review the legislative and administrative framework to ensure free and fair elections later this year and the religious leaders would make proposals to the government.

Earlier on Tuesday, students demanding constitutional reforms and the departure of Moi from office clashed with police in Kenya's capital in a second straight day of protests but the clashes were much lighter than on Monday
Kenyan opposition politician Richard Leakey said the Indian Ocean port city of Mombasa was the next target for the reform campaign.

"Moi must go. We want reforms," chanted hundreds of students from Kenya Polytechnic, ordered closed on Monday, as they built makeshift barricades on Haile Selassie Avenue, a major highway through Nairobi and only a block from the government centre.
In Mombasa, fiery Moslem preacher Sheikh Khalid Balala said he would urge people to burn voter registration cards from next Friday.
He has also called for a boycott of the presidential and parliamentary elections due this year.

"We shall take our message to the schools, hospitals and mosques and through the imams we will call on the people to burn the cards," said Balala, who was allowed to return to Kenya by authorities on Saturday after two years of exile in Germany.
He said voter cards would be burned every Friday from this week outside Sakina mosque in Mombasa and perhaps in Nairobi every Sunday until the government had agreed to the reforms.
On his return to Kenya, Balala vowed to spearhead the reform campaign but through his boycott call he has proved more extreme than opposition-backed groups organising protests since June.
Leakey told Reuters on Tuesday that Mombasa, the centre of Kenya's coast tourism industry, would be the next focus of the opposition-backed drive for reforms before the general election.

Leakey, secretary-general of the unregistered Safina party, said the committee behind the reform campaign sought government agreement by the end of July and realised protests in Mombasa could turn violent.
At least nine people were killed in Kenya on July 7 during the country's worst political violence in seven years when riot police broke up a day of demonstrations in favour of reforms.
The violence, which closed down Nairobi, was followed by several days of student unrest in the capital, prompting authorities to close indefinitely two universities.
The reforms demanded by the opposition before the elections would reduce the power of Moi, 73 and in power for 19 years.
